title: Bayesian Updating
tagline: Start with a belief, see evidence, update rationally — the mental engine of both trading and good answers.

concept.analogy: A good doctor doesn't diagnose from a single test. They start with how common a disease is (the base rate), then adjust based on the test result and how reliable that test is. A scary positive on a rare disease with an imperfect test often still means you're probably fine — because the base rate dominates. Bayesian updating is just doing that adjustment with arithmetic instead of gut feel, and it's exactly how a trader updates a price when news arrives.
paragraphs: Bayes' theorem tells you how to update the probability of a hypothesis H after seeing evidence E: P(H | E) = P(E | H)·P(H) / P(E). In words: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. Your prior P(H) is your belief before the evidence; the likelihood P(E | H) is how well the hypothesis explains the evidence; the posterior P(H | E) is your updated belief.

The denominator P(E) = Σ P(E | H_i)·P(H_i) is the total probability of the evidence across all hypotheses (law of total probability). A handy equivalent form uses odds: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. Updating in odds is often faster mentally.

The classic trap is base-rate neglect: people anchor on the test's accuracy and ignore how rare the condition is. With a rare disease, even a 99%-accurate test produces mostly false positives, so a positive result may leave you more likely healthy than sick. Interviewers use medical-test and similar problems precisely to see if you respect base rates.

In trading, Bayesian thinking is everywhere: your prior is the current fair value; a new trade, quote, or news item is evidence; you update your estimate of value and your quotes accordingly. Market-making games explicitly grade your Bayesian updating — do you revise your market as information arrives?
points: Bayes: P(H|E) = P(E|H)·P(H)/P(E); posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.
P(E) = Σ P(E|H_i)·P(H_i) — total probability across hypotheses.
Odds form: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio (fast for mental math).
Base-rate neglect: don't ignore how rare H is — rare priors dominate noisy evidence.
Trading = continuous Bayesian updating of fair value as evidence (flow, news) arrives.
concept.keyIdea: Update beliefs as posterior ∝ likelihood × prior, and never neglect the base rate. Whether diagnosing a disease or repricing an asset, the math is the same: weigh how surprising the evidence is against how likely the hypothesis was to begin with.

deepDive.intro: The mechanics, the odds shortcut, and the trader's framing.

steps.title: The formula and a worked medical test
steps.detail: Disease prevalence (prior) = 1%. Test: 99% true-positive, 5% false-positive. P(disease | positive) = (0.99·0.01)/(0.99·0.01 + 0.05·0.99) = 0.0099/(0.0099+0.0495) ≈ 0.167. A positive test still means only ~17% chance of disease — the rare base rate dominates.

steps.title: The odds shortcut
steps.detail: Prior odds of disease = 1:99. Likelihood ratio = P(+|disease)/P(+|healthy) = 0.99/0.05 ≈ 19.8. Posterior odds = (1:99)·19.8 ≈ 19.8:99 ≈ 1:5, i.e., ~1/6 ≈ 17%. Updating in odds avoids the denominator and is fast in your head.

steps.title: Sequential updating
steps.detail: Today's posterior becomes tomorrow's prior. Independent pieces of evidence multiply their likelihood ratios. This is how you incorporate a stream of signals — each one nudges the odds, and they compound.

steps.title: Calibration and overconfidence
steps.detail: Good Bayesians are calibrated: when they say 70%, they're right about 70% of the time. Interviewers (especially for trading) probe whether you update the right amount — not too little (anchoring) and not too much (overreacting to weak evidence). State your prior, state the evidence's strength, and move proportionally.

steps.title: The trading translation
steps.detail: Prior = current fair value / probability the price goes up. Evidence = a large buy print, a shift in book imbalance, a news headline. You ask 'how likely is this evidence if the price is about to rise vs. not?' and shift your estimate by that likelihood ratio. Overreact and you get whipsawed; underreact and you get picked off.

pitfalls: Base-rate neglect — anchoring on test accuracy and ignoring a rare prior.
Treating dependent evidence as independent (double-counting correlated signals).
Over- or under-updating: the size of the move should match the strength of the evidence.

practice.intro: Bayes problems are a staple. Do the arithmetic; the odds form is your friend under time pressure.

interviewQuestions.q: A disease affects 1 in 1000 people. A test is 99% accurate (1% false-positive rate, and detects all true cases). You test positive. What's the probability you have the disease?
a: So about 9% — despite a '99% accurate' test, a positive result more likely than not is a false alarm, because the disease is so rare. Odds check: prior odds 1:999, likelihood ratio 1/0.01 = 100, posterior odds ≈ 100:999 ≈ 1:10 ≈ 9%. Always respect the base rate.
followups: What if you test positive twice with independent tests?
How accurate must the test be for a positive to mean >50%?

interviewQuestions.q: A bag has two coins: one fair, one double-headed. You pick one at random and flip it; it lands heads. What's the probability it's the double-headed coin?
a: Prior: P(double) = P(fair) = 1/2. Likelihoods: P(heads|double) = 1, P(heads|fair) = 1/2.
P(double|heads) = (1·½)/(1·½ + ½·½) = (½)/(½ + ¼) = (½)/(¾) = 2/3. The heads result is evidence favoring the coin that always shows heads, lifting it from 1/2 to 2/3.

interviewQuestions.q: How is placing a tighter quote after seeing a burst of aggressive buying an act of Bayesian updating?
a: Your prior is the current fair value (say the mid/microprice) and your belief about the next move's direction. A burst of aggressive buying is evidence: it's much more likely to occur if the price is about to rise than if it isn't (a high likelihood ratio for 'up').

So you update your posterior toward 'price rising' and shift your fair value up. Acting on it, you raise/skew your quotes (lift your ask, maybe pull your bid) to avoid selling cheaply right before the rise — that's adverse-selection avoidance driven by a Bayesian update. The discipline is moving proportionally to the evidence's strength: a small flicker shouldn't move you much; a strong, sustained signal should.

problems.title: The classic base-rate (disease test) problem
problems.statement: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test is 99% accurate: it correctly flags 99% of sick people (sensitivity) and correctly clears 99% of healthy people (specificity, so 1% false-positive rate). You test positive. What is the probability you actually have the disease? Compute it and explain why the answer is so counterintuitive.
problems.hint: Bayes: P(sick|+) = P(+|sick)P(sick) / P(+). Compute P(+) from both sick and healthy contributions.

approach: Bayes: P(sick|+) = P(+|sick)·P(sick) / [P(+|sick)·P(sick) + P(+|healthy)·P(healthy)]. Plug in: P(sick)=0.001, P(+|sick)=0.99, P(healthy)=0.999, P(+|healthy)=0.01.

Despite a '99% accurate' test, a positive result means only ~9% chance of being sick. Why: the disease is rare (base rate 0.1%), so among any large group the *false positives from the huge healthy population* (≈1% of 999 ≈ 10 people per 1000) vastly outnumber the *true positives from the tiny sick population* (≈1 person per 1000). The base rate dominates. This is base-rate neglect — people anchor on the 99% accuracy and ignore the prior. The same reasoning applies in trading: a signal that 'fires correctly 99% of the time' is nearly worthless if the event it predicts is rare and false alarms are common; you must weight by the base rate.

problems.title: Updating belief about a coin's bias
problems.statement: A box has two coins: a fair coin (P(heads)=0.5) and a biased coin (P(heads)=0.8). You pick one at random (50/50) and flip it 3 times, getting H, H, H. What's the posterior probability you're holding the biased coin? Then: if the next flip is also heads, update again. Show the sequential Bayesian updating.
problems.hint: Likelihood of HHH under each coin; combine with the 50/50 prior. Then use the new posterior as the prior for the 4th flip.

approach: Prior: P(biased)=P(fair)=0.5. Likelihood of HHH: under fair = 0.5³ = 0.125; under biased = 0.8³ = 0.512. Posterior after HHH: P(biased|HHH) = (0.512×0.5)/(0.512×0.5 + 0.125×0.5) = 0.256/(0.256+0.0625) = 0.256/0.3185 ≈ 0.804. So three heads pushes belief from 50% to ~80% biased.

Sequential update on a 4th heads: use the posterior 0.804 as the new prior. P(biased|4th H) = (0.8×0.804)/(0.8×0.804 + 0.5×0.196) = 0.6432/(0.6432+0.098) = 0.6432/0.7412 ≈ 0.868. Belief rises to ~87%.

Equivalently you could compute it in one shot from HHHH likelihoods (0.8⁴ vs 0.5⁴ with the 0.5 prior) and get the same ~86.8% — sequential updating (posterior becomes the next prior) is mathematically identical to batch updating. This is exactly how a trader updates a market-making fair value or a 'is this flow informed?' belief tick by tick: start with a prior, multiply by the likelihood of each new observation, renormalize, repeat.

problems.title: The Monty Hall update
problems.statement: Three doors; a prize is behind one. You pick door 1. The host (who knows where the prize is and always opens a losing door you didn't pick) opens door 3, revealing no prize. Should you switch to door 2? Justify with Bayesian reasoning and state the win probabilities for staying vs switching.
problems.hint: Condition on the host's behavior. Your original pick was right with prob 1/3; the host's action transfers the rest.
problems.tests: Conditional probability and updating on an informative action.

approach: Switch. Initially P(prize behind your door 1) = 1/3, and P(prize behind doors 2 or 3 combined) = 2/3. The host's action is informative because he *always* opens a losing door among the ones you didn't pick. When he opens door 3 (empty), he's effectively concentrated that 2/3 probability onto the remaining unopened door 2.

Formally: P(win by staying) = P(your initial pick was correct) = 1/3 (the host's action gives no new info about your own door). P(win by switching) = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3. So switching doubles your win probability from 1/3 to 2/3.

The intuition that trips people up: the host isn't opening a door at random — he knowingly avoids the prize, so his choice carries information that updates your posterior. Treating his action as a conditioning event (not a random reveal) is the crux. This 'update on an informed party's action' is directly analogous to inferring information from an informed counterparty's trades in markets.
